strengths: The core idea is sensible and well-motivated: reformulating video object removal as a video-to-video bridge translation task leverages the input video as a structural prior, which addresses a genuine weakness of noise-to-data diffusion inpainting (incomplete erasure, implausible content, first-frame dependency bottlenecks).

The paper is clearly written and well-organized; the bridge formulation (Sec. 3-4) is presented with reasonable mathematical care, and the dual role of the source latent (prior boundary + spatial condition) is an intuitive design point.

The construction of a supplementary composite dataset (31k pairs with SAM2 foreground extraction and Qwen3-VL filtering) to complement the static-biased ROSE data shows awareness of the training-distribution problem and could benefit the community if released.

Qualitative results (Figs. 2-4) show competitive texture quality and temporal stability against GenOmnimatte, ROSE, and VACE, and the incidental removal of unmasked shadows is an interesting empirical observation.
The impact statement appropriately acknowledges misuse risks of video editing technology.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'significantly outperforming existing methods in visual quality and temporal consistency' is entirely unsupported by quantitative evidence. There are no numerical metrics (PSNR, LPIPS, FVD, temporal warping error), no user study, no evaluation benchmark is even defined (the test set and protocol are never specified), and no statistical analysis. The experimental section consists only of qualitative figures.

There are no ablation studies. The two claimed contributions - the VP-SDE bridge formulation and the adaptive mask modulation (AMM) - are never isolated: no comparison against a noise-to-data baseline under identical training, no ablation of AMM, and no analysis of the learned modulation parameter gamma. Claims that AMM 'counterbalances the strong source prior' or improves large-object removal remain speculative.

The AMM mechanism (Eq. 15) does not implement the motivation given for it. The paper motivates relaxing constraints for LARGE objects, but AMM is a single global learnable scalar applied to background embeddings; it does not condition on mask size or any 'mask characteristics' as claimed. This is a one-line feature-scaling trick presented as a novel contribution.

Key technical details required for verification and reproduction are missing: the solver weights w1, w2, w3 in Eq. 14 are said to be 'analytically determined' but never given; the velocity target derivation is deferred to an appendix that is not included in the manuscript. As written, Eq. 13 appears inconsistent with Eq. 11 (a factor of rho_t seems to be missing when recovering z_0|t from the velocity), and the correctness of the velocity target (Eq. 11) cannot be checked without the appendix.

The contribution is incremental: bridge models for data-to-data translation are established (I2SB, DDBM, BBDM, FrameBridge for I2V), and the paper is essentially an application of the Zhou et al. (2023a) bridge formulation on top of Wan2.1-1.3B with a mask-based input concatenation. The novelty over FrameBridge-style adaptation is limited.

Baseline selection is incomplete: DiffuEraser and Minimax-Remover, which the paper itself identifies as recent state-of-the-art removal methods, are cited but not compared. Training on a dataset that includes the ROSE data while evaluating primarily against ROSE raises fairness questions that cannot be assessed without a defined test protocol.

Presentation issues remain, including duplicated text ('leading to leading to'), figures without zoom-in regions or visual highlights to support the fine-grained quality claims, and anecdotal shadow-removal claims supported by only isolated frames rather than temporal sequences or analysis.

strengths: The core motivation is reasonable: leveraging the input video as a structural prior via a bridge formulation, instead of starting from Gaussian noise, is a sensible reframing of video object removal as video-to-video translation, and it is clearly argued in the introduction.
The paper is generally well written and easy to follow; the framework diagram (Figure 1) and the training/inference algorithms give a clear high-level picture of the pipeline.

The qualitative comparisons in Figures 2-4 suggest promising behavior, including the ability to remove unmasked collateral artifacts such as shadows, which is an interesting observation worth exploring.
The impact statement appropriately acknowledges the potential for misuse of video editing technology.
weaknesses: The central claim of the paper—'extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in both visual quality and temporal consistency'—is not supported by any quantitative evidence. There are no tables, no metrics (e.g., FVD, PSNR/SSIM, LPIPS, temporal warping error), no user study, and no evaluation protocol, test set, or number of test videos described. The experiments section contains only a qualitative comparison of cherry-picked frames against three baselines (GenOmnimatte, ROSE, VACE), and even omits DiffuEraser and Minimax-Remover despite both being cited as relevant SOTA removal methods. This is a fundamental evidential gap for a main-track submission.

There are no ablation studies whatsoever. The adaptive mask modulation (AMM) module—one of the two claimed contributions—is never evaluated; the learnable scalar γ is never reported, and there is no evidence it learns a meaningful value or improves performance over the plain bridge baseline. The claimed trade-off between strong bridge priors and large-object removal is asserted but never demonstrated.

The technical contribution is thin and derivative. The VP-SDE bridge formulation largely restates existing work (Zhou et al., 2023a; Tong et al., 2024), and AMM reduces to multiplying background patch embeddings by a single global learnable scalar (1+γ) (Eq. 15), which is called 'adaptive' and 'dynamically modulated based on mask characteristics'—language that oversells what is essentially one learnable constant. No analysis of how this interacts with self-attention (the 'soft bias' claim) is provided.

There are apparent inconsistencies in the derivations that undermine confidence in the math. The velocity target in Eq. 11 (ut = (at/ρt)ε − (ct/ρt)ztgt) contains no zsrc term even though the bridge state zt (Eq. 9) includes the time-dependent coefficient bt multiplying zsrc, whose time derivative should contribute to the velocity; the derivation is deferred to an appendix that is not included. The time convention is also inconsistent (t ∈ [0,1] with endpoints z0/z1 in Eqs. 2-4 and 9, but z0 ~ pdata and zT = zsrc in Eq. 7), and the direction of transport flips between Section 3 and Section 4.

Reproducibility is weak. The supplementary real-world composite dataset (31,000 pairs) is introduced but not released or described in enough detail to reconstruct (composite parameters, filtering thresholds, etc.), no code release is mentioned, and key details such as the exact solver weights w1, w2, w3 are only described as 'analytically determined' without formulas in the main text.

The claim that the model 'implicitly removes associated shadows even when they are not included in the input masks' is a notable claim presented purely via visual inspection, with no quantitative side-effect removal metric (e.g., against ROSE's evaluation protocol) to substantiate it.

The training setup (20,000 steps, 8 H100s, initialized from Wan2.1-1.3B) is reasonable, but the paper does not report inference time, memory, or compute comparisons with baselines, making it hard to judge the practical trade-off of the SDE-based sampler against distilled or few-step diffusion baselines.

strengths: The motivation is sound and well-argued: reframing video object removal as a video-to-video translation problem via a stochastic bridge, using the input video as a structural prior rather than starting from Gaussian noise, is a sensible and promising direction that addresses a real weakness of noise-to-data inpainting pipelines (e.g., the keyframe-guidance dependency bottleneck).

The paper is clearly written overall: the framework (Figure 1), the VP-SDE bridge interpolation (Eqs. 3, 9-10), the velocity-matching objective, and both training/inference algorithms are laid out with enough detail to follow, and I verified that the clean-latent inversion in Eq. 13 is algebraically consistent with the velocity target definition.

The identification of the fidelity-vs-flexibility trade-off introduced by a strong bridge prior, and the proposed Adaptive Mask Modulation (AMM) to address it, is a reasonable design insight, with an honest motivation for why the dual role of zsrc (prior + condition) can hinder large-object removal.

The data construction is described transparently, including the acknowledged bias of the ROSE dataset toward static objects and the composition-based pipeline (SAM2 foreground extraction, VLM-based filtering) used to build the supplementary 31k video-pair dataset.

Qualitative comparisons (Figures 2-4) against recent baselines (GenOmnimatte, ROSE, VACE) include scenarios with shadows/reflections outside the mask, and the claim that the model implicitly removes unmasked visual traces, if verified, would be a practically valuable property.
An impact statement discussing misuse risks of video object removal technology is included.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim — that the method 'significantly outperforms existing methods in both visual quality and temporal consistency' — is not supported by any quantitative evidence. The entire experimental section consists of three qualitative figure grids; there are no numbers for reconstruction quality (e.g., PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on the ROSE benchmark, which has ground-truth backgrounds), no temporal consistency metrics (e.g., warp-error/FVD), and no user study. Without at least quantitative results on the synthetic ROSE data where exact ground truth exists, the headline claim is unsupported.

There are no ablation studies. The claimed contribution of AMM is never validated: there is no comparison with/without AMM, no analysis of the learned modulation parameter γ, and no study of the sensitivity to the variance schedule β(t), the number of sampling steps, or the bridge vs. noise-to-data formulation on the same backbone. The trade-off motivating AMM (large objects failing under a rigid bridge prior) is also never demonstrated experimentally.

Several technical elements are under-specified or unverifiable: the derivation of the ground-truth velocity target (Eq. 11) is deferred to an appendix that is not included in the manuscript, and it is unclear why the target contains no zsrc-dependent drift term despite zt containing bt·zsrc; the solver weights w1, w2, w3 in Eq. 14 are said to be 'analytically determined' but never given; and the T5 text prompt is a required input at inference, yet the paper never specifies how prompts are constructed at test time or how sensitive results are to them.

The novelty is limited. The core generative machinery is a direct adaptation of existing VP/diffusion bridge formulations (Zhou et al., 2023a; I2SB; FrameBridge) to a new task on top of a pre-trained Wan2.1 backbone; AMM amounts to a single learnable scalar amplification of background embeddings. This could still be a useful contribution, but only with rigorous empirical validation, which is absent.

The evaluation protocol itself is undefined: no test set, number of test videos, or evaluation criteria are described, making the qualitative comparisons impossible to interpret or reproduce, and raising concerns about whether comparison samples were selected favorably.

Reproducibility is incomplete: implementation details are given, but no code or data release is mentioned, the composite training set construction depends on unreported filtering thresholds, and the missing appendix omits key derivations and solver weights.

The limitations discussion is superficial. Issues such as dependence on mask quality, prompt sensitivity, resolution/length constraints of the Wan backbone, potential leakage between the training composite data and test scenarios, and computational cost are not addressed in a dedicated discussion.

The writing contains noticeable errors that reduce polish, e.g., 'often leading to leading to', 'data,data generation paradigm', an inconsistent venue ('ICAIS, 2024' for Tong et al.), and Figure 2/3 both labeled 'Texture quality comparison' with no discussion in the text of what distinguishes them.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the VP-SDE bridge formulation for video object removal is coherent, with derivations of the bridge marginal, the guidance term h, and the equivalence between the velocity-matching loss and bridge score matching provided in the appendix.

Quantitative comparisons against six recent baselines (ROSE, VACE, GenOmnimatte, etc.) on DAVIS and a new 150-video benchmark show favorable results, with the largest gains on the authors' BridgeRemoval-Bench (e.g., +1.64 dB PSNR).

The introduction of BridgeRemoval-Bench, with landscape/portrait orientation, single/multi-object annotations, and three distinct video sources, is a useful community contribution given the acknowledged weakness of existing benchmarks.
The limitations section is honest and well-supported: the failure mode on fast-moving objects is illustrated (Figure 6) and shown to affect competing methods as well, rather than hidden.

A user study (24 participants, 1440 ratings) and VBench results are reported, and the authors appropriately explain why VBench has low discriminative power for this task rather than cherry-picking favorable metrics.
A practical speed/quality trade-off is demonstrated: 1.111 s/frame with 50-step sampling, faster than most baselines.
weaknesses: The central claim—that bridging from the source video is superior to the noise-to-data paradigm—is never directly tested. There is no ablation comparing BridgeRemoval against a flow-matching baseline trained with the same data, base model (Wan2.1-1.3B), and schedule. Appendix A only contrasts the two formulations conceptually (Table 3). Given that ROSE and VACE use the same base model and comparable data, this control experiment is feasible and its absence is the most serious evidential gap.

The AMM ablation (Appendix C.1) is qualitative only (a single bus example, Figure 4); no quantitative metrics are provided for the contribution claimed as the second main novelty, making it hard to assess its actual benefit.

Originality is incremental. The method is essentially DDBM (Zhou et al., 2023a) applied to latent video inpainting on top of Wan2.1, with an FiLM-style (Perez et al., 2018) mask modulation module; FrameBridge (Wang et al., 2025) already established bridge models for video synthesis with SNR-aligned fine-tuning. The paper positions itself as a 'paradigm shift,' which overstates the contribution.

Evaluation metrics are weak proxies for the task. CLIP-T against auto-generated captions is an unreliable measure of object removal, and PSNR/MSE/LPIPS computed only on unmasked regions largely reward background copying—a property the bridge prior provides by construction—so the headline PSNR gains may partly reflect the formulation rather than better inpainting.

Benchmark design risks self-favoritism: BridgeRemoval-Bench masks are produced with SAM2, the same segmentation pipeline used to build the authors' training data, and 50 of 150 test videos are Veo-generated synthetic clips, whose distribution may align with the composite training data.

Reproducibility is undermined by incomplete links: the project page and 'more samples' URLs are blank in the manuscript, and no code or data release is confirmed. The supplementary proofs in B.3 are also loose (using '∝' and informal equivalences rather than exact derivations).

Some results are less convincing than claimed: on DAVIS the improvements are marginal (e.g., LPIPS 0.0977 is worse than VACE's 0.0796; CLIP-F 0.9768 vs. Ditto's 0.9712), and the inference-step study (Table 4) shows differences within noise, suggesting low metric sensitivity.
Minor but numerous writing defects remain (e.g., 'often leading to leading to', 'can be visited at:' with no link), indicating the manuscript was not carefully finalized.

strengths: The paper is clearly written overall, with a complete description of the training objective, inference procedure, and pseudo-code for both training (Algorithm 4) and inference (Algorithm 6), and appendix derivations (B.1–B.3) that attempt to ground the coefficients in the DDBM framework.

The evaluation is fairly broad: comparisons against six recent methods on two datasets (DAVIS and the proposed BridgeRemoval-Bench), runtime comparison, a 24-participant user study, an inference-step analysis (Table 4, Figure 5), and VBench results reported in the appendix with an honest discussion of why VBench has limited discriminability for this task.

The limitation section (Appendix E) candidly identifies the fast-motion failure mode and shows comparable failures of competing methods on the same example, which is a fair and honest treatment of weaknesses.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core method is essentially the Denoising Diffusion Bridge Model (DDBM, Zhou et al., 2023a) re-applied to video object removal on top of a fine-tuned Wan2.1 backbone. The appendix derivation is largely a restatement of DDBM's known Gaussian bridge marginal, and the 'proof' that the specific coefficients at, bt, ct are valid is hand-waved ('This equality holds if we define the underlying diffusion schedule such that the SNR ratio matches...'). The Adaptive Mask Modulation is a fairly standard FiLM-style conditioning (Perez et al., 2018) on mask features. Neither contribution is a substantial methodological advance.

The central claim — that the bridge (source-to-target) formulation is superior to the noise-to-data formulation for object removal — is not directly tested. The crucial ablation (flow-matching baseline vs. bridge under the same data, base model, and training budget) is described conceptually in Table 3 and Algorithms 3/5, but no quantitative experimental result for this baseline is reported anywhere. The claimed superiority rests only on comparisons against prior methods with different training data, backbones, and pipelines.

The AMM ablation (Appendix C.1) is purely qualitative (a single video in Figure 4) with no quantitative results, weak evidence for a claimed key contribution. There is also a mild internal inconsistency: the appendix says AMM 'amplifies the embeddings in unmasked background regions' while the mechanism description (Eq. 15–17) modulates based on mask features across the whole frame, with no analysis of the learned gamma/beta.

Baseline numbers raise fairness concerns: Ditto, a strong method built on a larger Wan2.1-14B backbone, reports implausibly poor PSNR (11.73) and LPIPS (0.52) on DAVIS, which suggests possible reproduction or configuration issues rather than genuine method performance. Also, on DAVIS the proposed method actually loses to GenOmnimatte on CLIP-T (0.2788 vs. 0.2814), contradicting the blanket claim of 'significantly outperforming existing methods in both visual quality and temporal consistency.'

Potential evaluation bias: PSNR/MSE/LPIPS are computed only on unmasked regions, where the bridge formulation trivially reproduces the input outside the mask — this structurally favors the proposed paradigm and makes cross-paradigm comparisons of 'background preservation' less meaningful. CLIP-T against machine-generated captions (Qwen3-VL descriptions of 'object removed') is a weak proxy for object removal, and the captions were generated by the same pipeline used to build the authors' own benchmark.

The proposed benchmark uses SAM2-generated masks, which contradicts the introduction's claim of 'meticulously annotated masks'; using TikTok/stock videos also raises data licensing and consent questions that are not discussed in the impact statement.

Reproducibility and presentation gaps: the project page URL and the pointer to qualitative samples are literally blank in the manuscript ('The project page is', 'More samples can be visited at:'); no code release is stated; there are editorial errors (duplicated 'leading to leading to', 'ICIAS' for ICML in the Tong et al. citation, '2026' as a venue), and the abstract's incomplete URL. Training used only 20,000 steps on 8 H100s with limited detail on hyperparameter sensitivity.

The user study (24 participants, 1440 ratings) reports no statistical significance testing, and scores are rounded in a bar chart rather than a table, limiting the strength of the claimed human preference result.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated limitation of current diffusion-based video object removal: the noise-to-data paradigm discards the rich structural prior in the input video. Reformulating removal as a video-to-video bridge translation task is a sensible and coherent idea, well-connected to the DDBM / stochastic interpolants literature (Zhou et al., 2023a; Tong et al., 2024; FrameBridge).

The technical framework is clearly presented: the dual-role conditioning of the source latent (as both the bridge prior and a spatial condition) is a reasonable design, and the training/inference procedures are fully specified in Algorithms 1-6, including the variance-corrected SDE solver at inference.

Appendix B provides derivations connecting the specific coefficient schedule (a_t, b_t, c_t) to the general DDBM bridge marginal and shows the velocity-matching loss is equivalent to bridge score matching, giving the method a theoretical grounding rather than pure heuristics.

Empirical evaluation is fairly broad: six baselines on DAVIS and the new BridgeRemoval-Bench, favorable PSNR/LPIPS/CLIP-F results (e.g., +1.64 dB PSNR over the runner-up on their bench), runtime comparisons, a 24-participant user study, and VBench results in the appendix with a candid discussion of VBench's limited discriminability for this task.

The introduction of BridgeRemoval-Bench (150 videos across real, synthetic, and in-the-wild sources with landscape/portrait orientations and multi-object annotations) addresses a genuine gap, as existing benchmarks (DAVIS, ROSE-Bench) are small or lack standardized splits.

The limitations section (Appendix E) honestly identifies failure on fast-moving objects with ghosting artifacts and notes this is shared by competing SOTA methods, which is an appropriate treatment of limitations.
An ethics/impact statement is provided, acknowledging misuse risks of video manipulation technology.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core generative machinery is a direct application of the existing DDBM/VP-SDE bridge formulation to fine-tune Wan2.1, closely following FrameBridge's recipe of adapting bridge models to video foundation models. The AMM module is essentially FiLM conditioning driven by mask features, a standard technique. The contribution is more of a well-executed adaptation than a new method or new understanding.

The single most important controlled experiment is missing: a quantitative comparison of the bridge formulation against the noise-to-data flow-matching baseline under identical training data, base model, and schedule. The appendix compares the two only via pseudocode (Table 3, Algorithms 3-4), yet the central claim of the paper is that bridging is superior to noise-initialized generation. Without this ablation, the observed gains could be attributable to the new training data (47K pairs) or conditioning design rather than the bridge formulation itself.

The AMM ablation (Appendix C.1) is purely qualitative (one Figure 4 example). No quantitative ablation is reported for the paper's second main contribution, so its contribution to the reported metric gains cannot be assessed. Nor is there an ablation of the dual-role conditioning (source latent as prior vs. spatial condition).

Evaluation methodology has confounds and weaknesses: (i) CLIP-T against a generated caption of the object-removed video is a coarse and noisy proxy for 'object removed'; (ii) baselines use different base models (e.g., Ditto on Wan2.1-14B, ICVE on HunyuanVideo-13B) and different training data, so comparisons are not apples-to-apples; (iii) the authors introduce and use their own benchmark, whose SAM2-only masks are not reported to be human-verified, raising the possibility of a benchmark aligned with their method's characteristics.

The theoretical contribution in Appendix B largely restates known DDBM results; the justification that their specific (a_t, b_t, c_t) are a valid instance of Eq. 22 is somewhat hand-waved ('this equality holds if we define the underlying diffusion schedule such that the SNR ratio matches...'), without a rigorous derivation of that schedule.

Presentation issues undermine polish: notation inconsistency in Section 3 (p1 labeled 'source' in text but Eq. 1 says p1 is the prior transported from), a broken/unfilled project page URL and qualitative-results link ('More samples can be visited at:'), the typo 'L20X GPUs', an incomplete sentence in the introduction ('implausible content that conflicts with the scene's physical logic' missing punctuation), and the user study comparing only four of the seven methods without explaining the selection.

The composite training data pipeline (SAM2 segmentation + compositing) may introduce supervision artifacts (hard mask boundaries, missing shadows/reflections) whose effect on the learned removal behavior is not analyzed, especially given ROSE showed object side effects are a key difficulty.

Reproducibility is partial: implementation details (base model, schedule, optimizer, steps) are given, but no code release is stated, and links to data/benchmark construction details (mask quality checks, Qwen3-VL filtering thresholds) are absent.
